fragen.frage: Why is 6. Bc4 the right developing move here?
antworten: It defends the pawn on e4 against an attack by the knight on g8.
It prepares queenside castling.
It develops with a threat: bishop and queen attack f7, and only the king defends f7.
fragen.erklaerung: Black has to answer the threat against f7 and gains no time for development. So White pulls further ahead with every move.

fragen.frage: Why does White sacrifice a whole knight with 10. Nxb5?
antworten: It wins the pawn on b5 and keeps White ahead in material.
After Nxb5, the knight forks king and rook.
It opens lines against the king in the center while the black pieces are pinned and undeveloped.
fragen.erklaerung: After cxb5 Bxb5+, the bishop aims at the king on e8, and the bishop on g5 still pins the knight on f6. Black has more material; White has the pieces that take part in the game.

fragen.frage: Why does White castle queenside with 12. O-O-O?
antworten: The king gets to safety, and the rook attacks the pinned knight on d7 along the d-file.
Queenside castling stops Black from castling.
From d1, the rook defends the bishop on b5.
fragen.erklaerung: One move with two jobs: king safety and a new attacker. The knight on d7 is pinned to the king and cannot escape the pressure.

fragen.frage: Why is 15. Bxd7+ the start of the mate?
antworten: The bishop on d7 then defends the square c8 for the queen.
After the recapture Nxd7, the diagonal of the bishop on g5 is open as far as d8; Qb8+ and Rd8# follow.
Black has to recapture with the king and walks into a check from the rook on d1.
fragen.erklaerung: The knight on f6 stood on the diagonal g5–d8. If it recaptures, the bishop covers e7 and d8, and after the queen sacrifice the rook mates on d8.

fragen.frage: Why does the bishop sacrifice 12. Bxh7+ pay off here?
antworten: Black must not take the bishop, or else it is mate.
With the sacrifice, White heads into a better endgame.
Only the king defends h7, and knight and queen can follow up at once.

abschnitt.label: sec:k11-lasker
abschnitt.titel: Lasker–Thomas: the most famous king hunt

unterschrift.text: , White to move. Gold: the queen sacrifice on h7. Gray: behind the knight on e4, the bishop on d3 aims at h7.

fragen.frage: Why does Lasker sacrifice the queen with 11. Qxh7+?
antworten: After Kxh7, Nxf6+ gives double check with the knight and the bishop on d3.
The queen on h5 was attacked and had to move anyway.
This way White forces an endgame a pawn up.
fragen.erklaerung: Against a double check, only a king move helps. From then on, White hunts the king across the whole board, check after check.

fragen.frage: Why does White continue the hunt with 14. h4+?
antworten: The h-pawn is supposed to promote as quickly as possible.
White wants to drive the king back to g8.
Every move is check: Black never has time to make threats.
fragen.erklaerung: Forcing moves first: with nothing but checks, the calculation stays short and safe. Along the way, the king is driven deeper and deeper into White's camp.

fragen.frage: Why is 18. Kd2 mate, even though only the white king moves?
antworten: The king on d2 itself attacks the king on g1.
The king clears the first rank: the rook on a1 gives discovered check, and all escape squares are covered.
The rook on h2 gives check after the king move.
fragen.erklaerung: A discovered check: one piece moves away, and the piece behind it gives check. The rook on h2, the bishop on e2 and the knight on g4 cover the squares around the king on g1.

fragen.frage: Why is 6... exd4 not simply a gift for Black?
antworten: The pawn on d4 was undefended; Black wins it without any consequences.
Black wins material but gives White time and open lines against the king in the center.
This way Black forces White to trade queens.
fragen.erklaerung: In a gambit, White pays with pawns for time and activity. Whether the compensation is enough is shown by the factor balance; it changes with every move.

fragen.erklaerung: First stop the opponent's plan, then strike: without the sacrifice on c3, Black has no counterplay against the white king.

abschnitt.label: sec:k11-lautier
abschnitt.titel: Karpov–Lautier: the minority attack

unterschrift.text: The Carlsbad structure from Chapter 5, kings and pawns only, White to move. Gold: the advance b2–b4.

fragen.frage: Why does White advance the b-pawn in this structure, even though White has fewer pawns on the queenside?
antworten: White wants to create a passed pawn on the queenside.
After b4–b5 and the trade, Black is left with a weak pawn, for example on c6.
The advance protects White's own king.
fragen.erklaerung: This is the minority attack: two pawns attack three to create a weakness. The weakness ties Black down, and the win often comes on the other wing.

fragen.frage: Why does White trade both bishops with 13. Bxg6 and then Bxd6?
antworten: White wants to open the h-file for the rook.

fragen.frage: Why is the knight so well placed after 15. Ne5?
antworten: The guards of e5 have been traded, the pawn on d4 supports it, and the bishop on b7 behind d5 hardly takes part.

aufgabe.text: Morphy has sacrificed a knight for two pawns. Draw up a factor balance for this position as in Chapter 3: material, time, king safety, activity and durability. Does the sacrifice pay off?

loesung.text: White has given a knight for two pawns, so one point less.
White has three pieces in play (queen on b3, bishops on b5 and g5), Black two (queen on e7, knight on f6). Black is to move, but needs that move to parry the check.
The black king stands in check in the center and cannot castle kingside as long as the queen on e7 shuts in the bishop on f8. The white king, on the other hand, castles queenside next move.
The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6, and any piece that blocks the check on d7 is pinned there as well. The open d-file belongs to the white rooks.
Black would need three quiet moves to bring the king to safety; Black does not get that much time.
The sacrifice pays off, because Black could only have declined it with
and a queen trade. Even then, Black is at least a pawn down. Remember: one point of material weighs little if time, king safety and activity are on your side.

erklaerung.text: White has one point of material less, but more pieces in play, a safe king and the open d-file; the black king stands in check in the center, and anything that blocks the check gets pinned. Black does not get the three quiet moves needed: the sacrifice pays off.
